title: RBAC v2 Permission Inventory Methodology (Enumeration + Sensitivity Rubric)
author: Marcus Lin
body:
## Purpose
This document defines Redwood’s repeatable process for producing and maintaining a complete permission inventory for RBAC v2.

The inventory is the source of truth for:
- What actions exist across the control plane, console, admin/support tooling, and private deployment administration.
- Which actions are considered sensitive (P0/P1/P2) and why.
- Which RBAC v2 permission (resource + action + scope) gates each sensitive operation.
- What must be logged for auditability (who attempted what, whether it was allowed/denied, and why).

This methodology is designed to satisfy:
- Engineering needs (consistent enforcement + tests)
- Enterprise requirements (least privilege + separation of duties)
- Audit expectations (SOC 2/ISO evidence for access controls)

## Scope
### In-scope surfaces
Inventory must cover all externally- and internally-triggerable sensitive actions across:
- Control plane APIs (org, project, keys, models, deployments, rollouts, networking, integrations)
- Console backend endpoints (including “button clicks” that call internal APIs)
- Admin/support tooling (support impersonation, break-glass, internal admin APIs)
- Private deployment administration flows (installer/admin APIs, policy distribution/update)
- Audit log/export surfaces (enablement, configuration, export destinations, retention-affecting actions)

### Out-of-scope (initially)
- Data-plane/token-level inference authorization beyond tenant/project scoping (e.g., prompt-level ACLs)
- Identity provider redesign (SSO/SAML) beyond mapping claims/groups to roles

### Definitions
- **Action**: A discrete operation a caller can cause (e.g., “rotate API key”, “enable SSO enforcement”, “download audit log export”).
- **Sensitive action**: An action that changes access, exposes customer data, alters security posture, or materially impacts availability/cost.
- **Permission (RBAC v2)**: `(resource, action, scope)` tuple enforced by the shared authorization path.
- **Scope**: The boundary the permission applies to, e.g., `org`, `project`, `deployment`, `dedicated_pool`.

## Inventory outputs (what ‘done’ looks like)
The inventory must be captured in the shared inventory sheet (or equivalent structured dataset) and include:
- Every sensitive action (P0/P1/P2) with a stable identifier
- The triggering interface(s): API endpoint(s), UI route(s), CLI/internal tool entry points
- Current enforcement status (missing/partial/ok) and target RBAC v2 permission name
- Ownership and review status

### Completion criteria (per service / surface)
A service/surface is considered “inventory complete” when:
1) All routes/handlers capable of mutating state or returning sensitive data are enumerated.
2) Each enumerated route maps to:
   - an RBAC v2 permission name (or an explicit “no auth required” rationale)
   - a P-level (P0/P1/P2)
   - expected actor types (end-user, service account, support, SRE break-glass)
3) Gaps are captured as follow-up work items (missing checks, inconsistent behavior, missing audit logging).

## How to enumerate actions (step-by-step)
### Step 0 — Establish the boundary for the pass
For each inventory pass, explicitly state:
- Services included (e.g., `control-plane`, `console-backend`, `dedicated-admin`, `audit-log-exporter`)
- Environments/tier specifics (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private)
- Whether internal-only endpoints are included (they should be, if they can impact customer orgs)

### Step 1 — Seed from route discovery (automated)
Use the inventory crawler/script (see ENG-5382) to generate a starting list of:
- HTTP method + path
- Handler/controller name
- Service name
- OpenAPI operationId (if available)
- Tags / route group

Guidance:
- Treat OpenAPI as necessary but not sufficient: many sensitive actions are triggered by console internal calls or background jobs.
- Ensure discovery includes internal admin routers (often mounted under separate prefixes).

### Step 2 — Expand using “capability tracing” (manual)
Add actions not reliably visible in the route list:
- Background jobs/async workers that perform privileged operations on behalf of a user
- One-off admin scripts/tools used by Support/SRE (even if not in the normal control plane)
- Installer/upgrade hooks for Private that apply config/policy updates

Technique:
- Walk the Console: list every settings page and every destructive/high-impact button.
- Walk the API: list create/update/delete/rotate/revoke operations; list “export/download” actions.
- Walk Support/SRE runbooks: identify every operation that can mutate customer configuration or access.

### Step 3 — Normalize into “actions”
Convert endpoints/handlers into discrete actions. Rules:
- One action should represent a stable intent and should not be overly endpoint-specific.
- Prefer verbs that describe user intent (e.g., `apikey.rotate`) rather than implementation detail.
- If a single endpoint supports multiple intents via parameters, split into multiple actions if sensitivity differs (e.g., changing a project name vs toggling SSO enforcement).

### Step 4 — Classify sensitivity (P0/P1/P2)
Apply the rubric below. When in doubt, classify higher and request review.

### Step 5 — Propose RBAC v2 permission mapping
For each action, propose:
- Resource type (e.g., `org`, `project`, `apikey`, `audit_log_export`, `dedicated_pool`, `private_policy_bundle`)
- Action verb (e.g., `read`, `list`, `create`, `update`, `delete`, `rotate`, `export`, `impersonate`, `break_glass_grant`)
- Scope boundary (org/project/deployment/etc.)

### Step 6 — Capture audit logging requirements
For P0/P1 actions, specify the expected audit log event(s) and required authz decision fields:
- actor identity, actor type
- org/project/deployment identifiers
- permission evaluated + policy version
- decision (allow/deny) and reason code

### Step 7 — Peer review + sign-off
Follow the review workflow described below. Inventory is not “done” until reviewed.

## Sensitivity classification rubric (P0/P1/P2)
The P-level describes the risk of unauthorized or accidental execution of an action.

### P0 — Critical
An action is P0 if it enables or materially contributes to:
- Privilege escalation or access control bypass (role changes, policy changes, support impersonation)
- Exfiltration of sensitive customer data (audit logs, secrets, API keys, customer configs with credentials)
- Disabling security controls (SSO enforcement, MFA/2FA requirements, audit logging/export)
- Irreversible or high-blast-radius destructive changes (delete org/project, delete production deployments, wipe logs)
- Break-glass / incident override actions

Examples (P0):
- Assign/revoke Org Admin or Security Admin roles
- Create/rotate/revoke API keys or signing keys
- Configure SSO/SAML settings and enforce SSO-only login
- Initiate support impersonation session; grant break-glass elevated session
- Export audit logs to external destinations; change exporter credentials
- Modify Private policy bundle trust/signature settings

### P1 — High
An action is P1 if it:
- Changes production behavior with customer impact (latency/cost/availability) but is not directly privilege escalation
- Changes billing-relevant configuration or could create material spend
- Exposes moderately sensitive operational data (detailed usage analytics, deployment logs) beyond basic read-only visibility

Examples (P1):
- Change Dedicated autoscaling policies / GPU pool config
- Modify model rollout policies (canary, fallback) and traffic routing rules
- View per-request logs/traces that may contain customer prompts/metadata (when applicable)
- Change retention periods (non-security disabling) that affect operational forensics

### P2 — Moderate
An action is P2 if it:
- Is largely read-only or low-impact but still should be permissioned for least privilege
- Affects non-critical configuration or metadata

Examples (P2):
- View org/project settings (non-secret)
- List deployments/models without sensitive configuration values
- View billing invoices (may be P1 depending on customer policy; see notes below)

### Notes and edge cases
- **Billing data**: treat invoice download and payment method changes as P1/P0 depending on stored payment info access. Default to P1; escalate if payment instruments are involved.
- **Logs/traces**: if logs can include prompts or identifiers, treat log access as P1.
- **“Read” actions can be P0**: exporting audit logs, downloading key material, or reading secrets are P0 even though they are reads.

## Required metadata per inventory row
Each action must have the following fields populated.

### Identity + discovery fields
- **Action ID**: stable identifier used in the inventory (e.g., `CP-KEY-ROTATE-001`).
- **Proposed RBAC v2 permission name**: e.g., `apikey.rotate` on resource `apikey` in `project` scope.
- **Service**: e.g., `control-plane`, `console-backend`, `dedicated-admin`, `private-installer`.
- **Surface**: `api`, `console`, `admin_tooling`, `private_admin`.

### Invocation fields
- **Endpoint(s)**: HTTP method + path (include multiple if applicable).
- **Operation/handler**: controller name, function, job name, or CLI command.
- **UI entry point** (if any): Console page + button/action (e.g., `Settings → API Keys → Rotate`).

### Authorization fields
- **Current authn**: required identity type (end-user token, service account, internal admin).
- **Current authz status**: `missing`, `partial`, `ok`.
- **Required actor types** (select all):
  - End user (customer)
  - Service account (customer)
  - Support (Redwood)
  - SRE/on-call (Redwood)
  - Automated system (Redwood internal job)
- **Required approvals** (if any): e.g., break-glass approval, ticket link requirement.
- **Scope boundary**: org / project / deployment / dedicated_pool / global.

### Data + impact fields
- **Sensitivity**: P0 / P1 / P2.
- **Customer impact summary**: one sentence describing what could go wrong.
- **Data touched**: keys/secrets, billing, audit logs, deployment config, etc.

### Auditability fields
- **Audit event(s)**: event name(s) to emit.
- **Minimum audit fields**: actor, target resource ids, decision, reason code, policy version.
- **Retention class**: standard vs extended (if applicable).

### Ownership fields
- **Owner**: team/individual responsible for correctness of mapping.
- **Reviewers**: security + service owner.
- **Review status**: `not_started`, `in_review`, `approved`, `blocked`.

## Naming conventions (RBAC v2 mapping guidance)
### Permission naming
Use `resource.action` form with consistent verbs:
- Common verbs: `read`, `list`, `create`, `update`, `delete`, `rotate`, `revoke`, `enable`, `disable`, `export`, `impersonate`, `grant`.
- Avoid embedding environment-specific names unless the resource is tier-specific (e.g., `dedicated_pool.update`).

### Resource taxonomy guidance
- Prefer a resource that matches the user mental model and UI object (org, project, apikey, deployment, audit_log_export).
- If the endpoint mutates a sub-field of a resource with different sensitivity, consider splitting into a sub-resource (e.g., `org_sso_config.update` vs `org_profile.update`).

### Scope guidance
- If an action affects an entire organization (roles, SSO, audit exports), scope it to `org`.
- If an action is isolated to a project (API keys, model deployments in that project), scope it to `project`.
- Break-glass/support impersonation is always treated as `org` scope with additional controls.

## Review workflow (who approves what)
### Roles in the review
- **Service owner** (Engineering lead for the surface): confirms route completeness and correct semantics.
- **Security Engineering** (project owner): confirms sensitivity, least-privilege mapping, and separation of duties.
- **GRC** (as needed for P0-heavy surfaces): confirms evidence expectations for audits and customer questionnaires.

### Review stages
1) **Draft** (authoring): service owner populates inventory for their routes; marks unknowns explicitly.
2) **Security review**: Security Engineering reviews all P0/P1 and spot-checks P2.
3) **Resolution loop**: update mappings, split/merge actions, add missing actions.
4) **Approval**: mark actions as approved with reviewer names; file follow-up tickets for enforcement gaps.

### Required review thresholds
- P0: must be reviewed by Security Engineering + service owner.
- P1: must be reviewed by Security Engineering OR service owner (both preferred).
- P2: service owner review required; security review optional unless the surface is historically risky.

### Handling disagreements
If classification or mapping is disputed:
- Default to higher sensitivity (more restrictive) until resolved.
- Escalate to Security exec owner (Marcus Lin) for P0 policy disputes.
- Document rationale in the inventory notes column; link to any ADR/thread.

## Quality checks (common pitfalls)
Use this checklist during review:
- Are “read-only” exports correctly marked P0 (audit logs, keys, secret config downloads)?
- Are admin-only/internal endpoints included (support tooling, migration endpoints, backfills)?
- Are multi-tenant endpoints correctly scoped (org vs project)?
- Are actions that change security posture isolated (SSO enforcement, role changes, policy updates)?
- Are we missing UI-driven actions that call internal endpoints?
- Are reason codes defined for 403 responses for P0/P1 actions?

## Example inventory rows (illustrative)
Example A — API key rotation
- Service: control-plane
- Endpoint: POST /v1/projects/{project_id}/apikeys/{key_id}:rotate
- Action: `apikey.rotate`
- Scope: project
- Sensitivity: P0
- Actors: End user, Service account (if supported)
- Audit event: `apikey.rotated` (include actor, project_id, key_id, policy_version, allow/deny)

Example B — Dedicated autoscaling update
- Service: dedicated-admin
- Endpoint: PATCH /v1/dedicated/pools/{pool_id}/autoscaling
- Action: `dedicated_pool.update_autoscaling`
- Scope: org (or dedicated_pool scope if modeled)
- Sensitivity: P1
- Actors: End user
- Audit event: `dedicated.autoscaling.updated`

Example C — Support impersonation
- Service: admin_tooling
- Entry point: Support console → “Impersonate user”
- Action: `support.impersonate`
- Scope: org
- Sensitivity: P0
- Actors: Support (Redwood)
- Approvals: required (ticket + time-bounded grant)
- Audit events: `support.impersonation.granted`, `support.impersonation.started`, `support.impersonation.ended`

## Ongoing governance (after initial inventory)
### When a new endpoint/action is added
Engineers adding new routes/handlers that:
- mutate state, OR
- return sensitive data, OR
- affect access/security posture,

must:
1) Declare an RBAC v2 permission mapping in code (per authz-check standard).
2) Add/confirm the action exists in the inventory.
3) Add/confirm audit logging for P0/P1.

### Periodic review cadence
- Quarterly: Security Engineering + service owners review new actions and re-evaluate P-levels.
- Prior to major enterprise launches: run a focused re-audit of P0/P1 for impacted surfaces.

### Evidence for audits / customer security reviews
For P0/P1 actions, be prepared to produce:
- Inventory excerpts showing classification and permissions
- Example audit log entries demonstrating authz decision context
- Screenshots of console role assignment (as applicable)

## Ownership
- Document owner: Security Engineering (Marcus Lin)
- Day-to-day inventory coordination: Authz implementation lead (Kaitlyn Nguyen)
- Audit logging alignment: Kevin Osei
